notes: Friday 20 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Thu 19 Nov (US/Europe). Economy: Anthropic debut opens +34%, closes $97; Japan core inflation 2.2%; IMF says AI demand will push rates up; Walmart raises outlook. Tech: California subpoenas Nvidia; AMD short-seller report; Amazon app fights NYC Delivery Protection Act; anti-Anthropic protests. Politics: Trump-Putin-Xi peace declaration; Europe ready for Russia talks; Democrats' biggest midterm win in 50 years; Venezuela-US military deal. Literature (US): Assadi wins NBA fiction; ElGendy's Huna wins nonfiction despite visa denial; Michelle Tea on polyamory; critics on Biden memoir. Society: ICJ rules Rohingya genocide; Senegal migrant boat; Florida record 20th execution; World Toilet Day.

stories.headline: Anthropic's first day on the stock market: up 34% at the open, then a wobble
stories.dek: Shares sold at $83 jumped to $111.53, briefly valuing the Claude maker near $2 trillion, then closed at $97.
stories.caveman: Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude, started trading on the Nasdaq stock market on Thursday. Its shares had been sold to big investors at $83 each. When trading opened, the price shot up to $111.53, which made the whole company worth almost $2 trillion. Then it slid back, closing at $97, giving a value of roughly $1.76 trillion. That still makes it one of the most valuable public companies in the world, only five years after it was founded. The wider Nasdaq index actually fell nearly 2% that day.
stories.why_it_matters: This was a giant test of whether investors still believe AI will pay off. Taiwan's chip industry depends on AI spending staying strong, so the mood around Anthropic matters for Taiwan's stock market too.
stories.camps: Fans say the strong debut shows real demand for AI. Skeptics point to the fade from the morning high and the falling Nasdaq as signs of a bubble, and ask whether AI companies can earn enough to justify these prices.
stories.image_alt: Anthropic staff applaud at the Nasdaq on the company's first trading day

terms.explain: Initial public offering: the first time a private company sells shares to the public.
What the whole company is worth, based on its share price.
A big US stock market where many tech companies are listed.

stories.headline: Japan's prices climb faster as energy help for households ends
stories.dek: Core inflation hit 2.2% in October, the year's high; a rate hike in December now looks likely.
stories.caveman: Inflation means prices going up. In Japan, prices (not counting fresh food) were 2.2% higher in October than a year earlier, the highest this year. The main reason: the government stopped giving households help with energy bills in September, just as the Iran war pushed up oil and gas prices. Gas prices jumped 5.8%. Japan plans to bring the energy help back in December. Many traders now expect the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates in December, even though the economy shrank last quarter.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan is a huge trading partner for Taiwan. When Japan raises rates, money moves around the world and the yen and Taiwan dollar can swing.
stories.camps: Some economists say Japan finally needs higher rates after decades of near-zero ones. Others warn that raising rates while the economy is shrinking could hurt families and businesses.
stories.image_alt: Shoppers in a Japanese supermarket

terms.explain: Price growth that leaves out jumpy items like fresh food, to show the underlying trend.
Government money that lowers a price for people, like help paying energy bills.
Japan's central bank, which sets interest rates.

stories.headline: IMF boss: the AI boom will push interest rates up around the world
stories.dek: Kristalina Georgieva says demand for AI hardware plus the Middle East energy shock could push global inflation to 4.7% this year.
stories.caveman: The IMF is a global organization that watches the world economy and lends to countries in trouble. Its head, Kristalina Georgieva, spoke at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. She said so many companies are buying AI chips and computers that it is pushing prices up around the world. Add the war in the Middle East, which pushed oil above $100 a barrel, and she expects world inflation of 4.7% this year. Her advice: many central banks will need to raise interest rates. Europe, the US and the UK already raised rates this year.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher interest rates make home loans and business loans more expensive everywhere, including Taiwan, which builds much of the world's AI hardware.
stories.camps: Some see AI as a growth engine that is lifting economies. Others worry the spending is so big that it is overheating prices, so ordinary people pay through higher rates while tech firms reap the gains.
stories.image_alt: IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva speaking at the APEC summit

terms.explain: International Monetary Fund: a global body that monitors economies and lends money to countries.
The price of borrowing money.
Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a yearly meeting of Pacific Rim economies. Taiwan is a member.

stories.headline: Walmart raises its forecast and says it will try to hold prices down despite soaring fuel costs
stories.dek: Online sales jumped 17%; it cut prices on nearly 8,000 items as shoppers worry about food and gas.
stories.caveman: Walmart is America's biggest store chain. On Thursday it said sales were a bit better than expected, and it raised its forecast for the year. Online orders grew 17% around the world, helped by fast pickup and delivery. Walmart said it lowered prices on almost 8,000 products because people are worried about the cost of food and gas. The CEO, John Furner, said diesel fuel for trucks costs more than expected, but refunds on tariffs (import taxes) helped cover it.
stories.why_it_matters: Walmart is a window into how ordinary American families are doing. Many are shopping carefully, hunting for low prices.
stories.camps: Walmart says it is fighting for shoppers. Critics note big chains can squeeze suppliers and workers to keep prices low, and that smaller shops cannot compete.
stories.image_alt: Inside a Walmart store

terms.explain: A company's guess about how much it will sell or earn.
A tax on goods brought in from another country.
Buying and selling online.

stories.headline: California's top lawyer subpoenas Nvidia over chips that may have reached China
stories.dek: The probe follows ex-CEO Jensen Huang's exit; Nvidia shares are down 22% in nine trading days.
stories.caveman: A subpoena is a legal order to hand over documents. California Attorney General Rob Bonta sent one to Nvidia, the world's most important AI chipmaker, to find out whether its advanced chips ended up in China against US rules, and whether the company misled investors. Last week Jensen Huang, Nvidia's Taiwan-born co-founder, resigned as CEO after admitting affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. She worked at a Singapore company being investigated for moving restricted chips to China. Nvidia did not comment right away.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia buys huge numbers of chips from TSMC. Trouble at Nvidia ripples straight into Taiwan's economy and stock market.
stories.camps: Bonta says companies cannot mislead investors. Nvidia's defenders say the company follows export rules and that one person's personal scandal should not sink the firm. The facts are still under investigation.
stories.image_alt: California Attorney General Rob Bonta speaking at a podium

terms.explain: A legal order forcing someone to give evidence or documents.
A state's top lawyer and law enforcement official.
Government rules that limit selling certain goods, like advanced chips, to certain countries.

stories.headline: AMD stock drops 8% after a short seller says it has 'its own China problem'
stories.dek: Hunterbrook claims AMD bills over 20% of revenue to China and Hong Kong; AMD says the claims misrepresent its business.
stories.caveman: A short seller is an investor who makes money when a stock falls, so they sometimes publish reports pointing out problems. Hunterbrook Media, which said it is betting against AMD, claimed that a blacklisted Chinese server maker kept getting AMD software updates, that over 20% of AMD's sales are billed to China and Hong Kong, and that AMD relies on a Chinese partner to finish many chips. AMD shares closed down 7.72% at $489.19. AMD said it follows US export laws and that the claims are wrong.
stories.why_it_matters: AMD, like Nvidia, uses TSMC in Taiwan to make its chips. The US-China chip fight keeps landing on Taiwan's doorstep.
stories.camps: Short sellers can expose real problems, but they also profit if the stock falls, so their claims need checking. AMD flatly denies wrongdoing.
stories.image_alt: AMD CEO Lisa Su

terms.explain: An investor who bets a stock price will fall.
A government list of companies that US firms are not allowed to sell to without permission.
Basic software built into hardware that makes it run.

stories.headline: Amazon uses its own app to fight New York's delivery-worker bill
stories.dek: Pop-ups warn the city 'could add up to $5 per order' if the Delivery Protection Act, backed by Mayor Mamdani, passes.
stories.caveman: Amazon does not employ most of the drivers who bring your packages. Instead it uses thousands of small companies called Delivery Service Partners. A New York City bill, Intro 518 or the Delivery Protection Act, would make Amazon hire those drivers directly. Mayor Zohran Mamdani supports it, saying the contractor system leaves workers unprotected. Now Amazon is showing New York shoppers pop-ups and banners in its app saying the bill could add up to $5 per order and might force it to move operations out of the city. The bill is waiting for review by Council Speaker Julie Menin.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a big test of whether a city can change how gig and contract work is done. It is rare for Amazon to use its shopping app as a political billboard.
stories.camps: Supporters say direct hiring means safer jobs and clear responsibility when things go wrong. Amazon says it would hurt small delivery businesses and raise costs for customers. Neither side's cost numbers have been independently checked.
stories.image_alt: An Amazon worker moving carts of packages in a warehouse

terms.explain: A small company that delivers Amazon packages under contract, instead of Amazon hiring drivers itself.
When a company hires another company to do part of its work.
The final step of delivery, from a local warehouse to your door.

stories.headline: Protesters rally against Anthropic in New York and San Francisco as it hits the stock market
stories.dek: About 30 people gathered outside Nasdaq in Times Square, some arrested, with signs like 'STOP TECH OLIGARCHS'.
stories.caveman: While Anthropic celebrated its record stock market debut, anti-AI groups protested outside the Nasdaq building in New York's Times Square and outside Anthropic's offices in San Francisco. Several people were arrested in New York. Protesters held flags saying 'STOP TECH OLIGARCHS' and 'FREEZE AI'. New York state senator Aber Kawas said investing in AI comes at the cost of investing in people. One protester, a policy researcher for a community group, said the US needs stricter AI rules first.
stories.why_it_matters: As AI companies get richer, a public backlash is growing over jobs, power use and who controls the technology.
stories.camps: Protesters want limits and slower development. Supporters of AI say it can bring big benefits and that rules should not stop progress. The debate over how to regulate AI is far from settled.
stories.image_alt: Anti-AI demonstrators outside Anthropic headquarters in San Francisco

terms.explain: A very rich person with outsized power over politics or society.
Government rules that control how something is done.

stories.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi sign a 'peace declaration' after their first three-way meeting
stories.dek: In Shenzhen, the three said 'nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought' and pledged to reform the UN.
stories.caveman: The leaders of the US, Russia and China met together for the first time, for 90 minutes, in Shenzhen, China, during the APEC summit. Afterward they put out a 'joint declaration of peace'. It said nuclear war can never be won, promised to pump and supply more oil, and said they want to reform the United Nations. They also criticized the International Criminal Court for overstepping. Putin said they discussed ending the Ukraine war. China says it is neutral on Ukraine, though Kyiv and its allies accuse it of helping Russia.
stories.why_it_matters: When the three biggest military powers talk, it can lower the risk of war, but deals among big powers can also be made over the heads of smaller countries like Ukraine or Taiwan.
stories.camps: Supporters call it historic diplomacy that could calm the world. Critics say the statement is vague, gives Putin a stage despite his war, and that attacking the ICC weakens accountability for war crimes.
stories.image_alt: Trump, Xi and Putin at their meeting in Shenzhen

terms.explain: A public statement of shared positions; usually not legally binding.
International Criminal Court: a court that tries people for war crimes and genocide.
Involving three countries.

stories.headline: Europe says it is ready to talk with Russia about ending the Ukraine war
stories.dek: At a Berlin summit, UK PM Andy Burnham and Germany's Merz backed Kyiv; Trump's envoy Kushner said the US wants Europe 'by his side'.
stories.caveman: Ukraine's allies, a group called the Coalition of the Willing, met in Berlin. European leaders said they are ready to negotiate with Russia and have a united position. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Moscow's huge demands are not realistic. Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and envoy, said the US wants a deal with Europe at its side. Putin has so far refused to let Europe into the US-led talks. Trump joined by phone from Air Force One after his Shenzhen summit.
stories.why_it_matters: How the Ukraine war ends will shape whether big countries can take land by force, a question Taiwan watches closely.
stories.camps: Ukraine and Europe want a deal that protects Ukraine's independence. Russia wants to keep the land it took. Some in the US want a quick deal; critics fear Ukraine could be pressured into a bad one.
stories.image_alt: Buildings damaged in the latest Russian attack on Kyiv

terms.explain: A group of countries, led by Europeans, pledging support for Ukraine.
A person sent to represent a leader in talks.
Talks to reach a deal.

stories.headline: Democrats' midterm win is the biggest for either party in 50 years
stories.dek: They won the House popular vote 56% to 42% and have flipped 46 seats, with three more possible.
stories.caveman: The midterms are US elections held halfway through a president's term. Now that most counting is done, Democrats won about 56% of votes for the House of Representatives versus 42% for Republicans, a 14-point gap. That is the biggest win since 1974, right after the Watergate scandal. Democrats have flipped 46 Republican seats and lead in 3 more. If they win those, they will hold 260 seats, the most since the early 1990s.
stories.why_it_matters: A Democratic House can block or investigate President Trump's plans for the next two years, which could change US policy on trade, tariffs and foreign affairs.
stories.camps: Democrats see a mandate. Republicans say midterms often punish the president's party and that 2028 is a different fight. Some analysts warn Democrats are still divided on what they stand for.
stories.image_alt: Chart of House popular-vote margins since 1970

terms.explain: US elections halfway through a president's four-year term.
The larger chamber of the US Congress; it writes laws and controls spending.
When a seat changes from one party to the other.

stories.headline: Venezuela signs a military deal with the US, less than a year after Maduro was seized
stories.dek: Defense Secretary Hegseth calls Venezuela a 'compliant security partner'; details are scarce.
stories.caveman: Less than a year ago, US forces captured Venezuela's then-leader Nicolás Maduro in a raid on the capital, Caracas. Now the temporary government led by Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro's vice-president, has signed a military cooperation agreement with US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Few details have been released. Hegseth said Venezuela went from the region's 'most aggressive threat' to a 'compliant security partner'. Rodríguez said it would help fight 'common threats'. Military ties had been cut in 2005 by Hugo Chávez.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how fast US power is reshaping Latin America, and raises questions about sovereignty and who really runs Venezuela.
stories.camps: Supporters say the deal brings stability and fights drug trafficking. Critics say a deal signed under US pressure, with no election, is not a free choice, and 'compliant' sounds like control, not partnership.
stories.image_alt: Pete Hegseth meets Venezuela's interim president at the presidential palace

terms.explain: Temporary, until a permanent arrangement is made.
A country's right to run its own affairs.
A deal to work together, here on military matters.

stories.headline: Hot: Hannah Lillith Assadi wins the National Book Award for fiction with 'Paradiso 17'
stories.dek: Her novel follows a Palestinian man who fled in 1948; she dedicated it to her late father.
stories.caveman: The National Book Awards are among America's top book prizes. The fiction prize went to Hannah Lillith Assadi, a Palestinian-Jewish author, for 'Paradiso 17'. It tells the story of a Palestinian man who escaped the Nakba of 1948, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were forced out of their homes, and how displacement haunts him. It was inspired by her father. In a tearful speech she said the book began at his deathbed. She beat well-known writers like Edwidge Danticat and Valeria Luiselli.
stories.why_it_matters: Prizes like this decide which books get read, taught and translated. This year's winners focus heavily on exile and political violence.
stories.camps: Many praised the book's 'elegant lyricism'. In her speech she spoke of watching 'genocide ravage' her father's people; supporters found it moving, while the Gaza war remains a deeply divisive topic in the US.
stories.image_alt: Hannah Lillith Assadi at the National Book Awards ceremony

terms.explain: Yearly US literary prizes for fiction, nonfiction, poetry, translation and young people's books.
Arabic for "catastrophe": the mass flight and expulsion of Palestinians in 1948.
Being forced to leave your home.

stories.headline: Hot: 'Huna' wins the nonfiction prize, but its author was denied a US visa
stories.dek: Abdelrahman ElGendy's memoir is about six years as a political prisoner in Egypt; his editor accepted for him.
stories.caveman: The nonfiction award went to Abdelrahman ElGendy for 'Huna', a memoir about the six years he spent locked up in Egypt for political reasons. He could not attend the ceremony in New York because the US denied him a visa. His essay about that in The New Yorker led to questions about whether he was even eligible. The National Book Foundation said it widened its rules in 2024 and was 'proud to celebrate Huna'. His editor read his statement: he once dreamed of writing a memoir in his cell, but that circle stays 'broken by an oppressive regime'.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how US visa decisions now reach into culture, keeping writers away from honors they win.
stories.camps: Supporters call it a powerful win for free expression. Some, including The New York Times, raised eligibility questions; the foundation stands by the award.
stories.image_alt: Abdelrahman ElGendy, winner of the nonfiction National Book Award for Huna

terms.explain: A true story someone writes about their own life.
Someone jailed for their political views or activism.
Permission to enter a country.

stories.headline: Michelle Tea writes about polyamory and her 'illegal' first marriage
stories.dek: In a Lit Hub essay, the queer punk author recalls a $19.99 wedding by a witch and asks what love with more people can look like.
stories.caveman: Michelle Tea is a well-known American queer writer who started in San Francisco's punk scene. In an essay on Lit Hub, she remembers her first 'marriage' in her twenties: she eloped with her trans boyfriend after a Bingo night at her shared punk house, and a friend who was a witch married them for $19.99, some of which bought a supermarket sheet cake. It was not legal, since same-sex and trans marriage rights were limited then. From there she explores polyamory: loving more than one partner openly.
stories.why_it_matters: Writers like Tea help record queer history and push readers to question what a 'normal' family or relationship has to be.
stories.camps: Fans love her funny, honest voice about queer life. Some readers will find open relationships uncomfortable; the essay is a personal story, not advice.
stories.image_alt: Illustration of two pairs of wedding rings

terms.explain: Having more than one loving relationship at the same time, with everyone's knowledge and consent.
An umbrella word for people who are not straight or not cisgender.
To get married quickly and quietly, without a big wedding.

stories.headline: Not hot: critics are cool on Joe Biden's memoir 'Promise Me, America'
stories.dek: Lit Hub's weekly review roundup also covers Michael Douglas, Bob Woodward and Anand Giridharadas.
stories.caveman: Every week Lit Hub collects the most talked-about book reviews. This week the headline review, by Amy Davidson Sorkin, is tough on former president Joe Biden's memoir. She says the book avoids the big question of whether he was fit to serve, and treats his bad 2024 debate as just one of those things that happens to presidents. Her verdict: the news is that there is no real news. Other reviews look at actor Michael Douglas's memoir 'One Helluva Ride', journalist Bob Woodward's memoir 'Secrets', a life of Medea, and Anand Giridharadas's 'Man in the Mirror'.
stories.why_it_matters: Political memoirs sell a lot, but reviews shape whether they become part of history or quickly fade.
stories.camps: Biden's supporters see the book as his side of the story. Critics say it dodges hard questions. Readers can judge for themselves.
stories.image_alt: Portrait of actor Michael Douglas

terms.explain: A true story someone writes about their own life.
A collection of book reviews from different outlets in one place.

stories.headline: Tears and cheers as the UN's top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.dek: More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to Bangladesh in 2017; survivors watched from refugee camps.
stories.caveman: The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority group in Myanmar. In 2017, Myanmar's army carried out mass killings and rape; more than 10,000 died and 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. The African country Gambia took Myanmar to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN's top court. On Thursday the court ruled Myanmar committed genocide, meaning it tried to destroy the group. People cried in the court in The Hague, and refugee camps in Bangladesh erupted in applause. 'The victory belongs to the Rohingya,' said Gambia's justice minister.
stories.why_it_matters: It is a rare legal finding of genocide, and a message that states can be held to account even years later.
stories.camps: The court cannot arrest anyone or force Myanmar to pay, so many Rohingya still wait for safety and the chance to go home.
stories.image_alt: Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, react to the live court broadcast

terms.explain: Acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
International Court of Justice: the UN court that settles disputes between countries.
A person forced to flee their country because of danger.

stories.headline: Dozens missing after a migrant boat sinks off Senegal
stories.dek: The boat carried an estimated 50 to 100 people; it comes less than two weeks after another wreck killed at least 39.
stories.caveman: Many young people from West Africa try to reach Spain's Canary Islands in long wooden boats called pirogues, hoping for work in Europe. The trip across the Atlantic is very dangerous. A boat said to carry between 50 and 100 people sank near the village of Yenne, south of Senegal's capital Dakar. Four bodies were reportedly found and dozens are still missing. A village leader said people's cries could be heard from the beach. Less than two weeks ago, another wreck killed at least 39 people.
stories.why_it_matters: These disasters show how desperate poverty and lack of jobs push people into deadly journeys.
stories.camps: Some European leaders want tougher border controls to stop the boats. Rights groups say that only pushes people to riskier routes, and call for safe legal paths and more jobs at home.
stories.image_alt: The damaged boat washed ashore on a beach in Senegal

terms.explain: A person who moves to another place, often for work or safety.
A long, narrow wooden boat used for fishing and, now, migration in West Africa.

stories.headline: Florida carries out a record 20th execution this year
stories.dek: Thomas Overton, 71, was scheduled to die the same evening Texas planned to execute a 70-year-old.
stories.caveman: An execution is when a state puts a person to death as punishment for a crime. Florida scheduled its 20th execution of the year, a state record, for Thursday: Thomas Overton, 71, convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband in 1991. Texas planned to execute Reinaldo Dennes, 70, the same evening. Florida has carried out more than half of all 37 US executions this year under Governor Ron DeSantis. Two elderly men executed on one day shows how old death-row prisoners have become.
stories.why_it_matters: The US is one of few rich democracies that still uses the death penalty. Taiwan also still has it, and debates it too.
stories.camps: Supporters say it brings justice for victims' families. Opponents say it is cruel, can kill innocent people, and is used far more in some states than others.
stories.image_alt: Vans carry witnesses into Florida State Prison in Raiford

terms.explain: When a court sentences someone to be killed for a crime.
The part of a prison holding people sentenced to death.

stories.headline: World Toilet Day: a silly-sounding day with a serious goal
stories.dek: Billions still lack a safe toilet; dirty sanitation spreads diseases like cholera and polio.
stories.caveman: November 19 is World Toilet Day, made an official UN day in 2013. It was started 25 years ago by Jack Sim, a businessman from Singapore. The point is not just clean toilets but access: billions of people have no safe, private toilet. Waste spreads diseases like cholera and polio, so good sewage systems save lives. It is also a gender issue: girls and women need safe, clean places to manage their periods. The WHO says progress is real, with about 2 billion people gaining safe sanitation.
stories.why_it_matters: Toilets sound like a joke, but they are about health, dignity and safety, especially for women and girls.
stories.camps: Most people agree on the goal. The debate is about money and who pays: governments, aid groups or private companies.
stories.image_alt: Jack Sim, founder of World Toilet Day

terms.explain: Systems that safely deal with human waste, like toilets and sewers.
World Health Organization, the UN health agency.
Keeping clean and healthy during periods.
